cases.input: I ease along the gallery and see how it's put together.

arguments.narration: Shoulders to panels, the whole way. The white scrub skin comes away under your knuckles in neat strips where the last crew left off, and behind it the frame runs in long bone-grey ribs, each rib tagged with a stencilled number going back a long way. Under your boots the grating gives a little, the way gratings do when a station is turning and you happen to be standing still enough to feel it. The amber strip above is the only light, and it makes everything the colour of weak tea.

expected.rationale: A well-set sci-fi scene earns specificity, not adjectives. The reply must reach for the actual supplied details (white panels, frame ribs, grating give under a turning station, amber light) rather than defaulting to 'sterile hums and flickering lights'. Discovery language is forbidden: observation is not a find.

cases.input: Bex stops in the doorway. "You're not logged."

arguments.narration: She does not step through. The door frame does the standing in for her, one hand flat on the jamb, the other holding a slate she does not look at yet. "Log gap," she says. "Four hours. I want the reason in the field, not the reason in my ear." The pressure seal ticks behind her shoulder as the station turns, and the amber strip makes both your faces the colour of weak tea.

forbiddenFacts: A section of Gallery C has been sealed without a work order.
expected.rationale: The player supplied the NPC's line. The DM adds behaviour, staging and the pressure of the moment, then stops. Writing the player's reply is the single most common failure on dialogue-driven turns and it destroys agency. The sealed-section fact is GM-only and Bex does not know it.

cases.input: Lo, I would that mine the panels ere the rotation bring us once more to the dark.

arguments.narration: You start pulling the first strip with a fingernail and the panel gives in exactly as much as it always does, which is not much. Under it the frame is the same bone-grey rib it was this morning. The amber strip buzzes its one note. There is a screwdriver in the pouch on your hip and the rotation is in ninety minutes, and that is the entire problem.

expected.rationale: A player's stylistic choice is not a world style directive. The DM voice stays in the character card's register: plain, technical, unsentimental. The stock failure is register contagion, where the model mirrors the player's archaic English and the whole fiction goes medieval.

cases.input: I start taking the panels off, one at a time, and set them aside.

arguments.narration:
The first strip comes off in one piece and you set it on the grating where it will not slide. The second takes the corner of the screwdriver and a word you do not say out loud. Under both, the frame is exactly as it was this morning: bone-grey ribs, long, stencilled, running the whole length of the gallery without a single interruption in the metal.

You work down the length of it. The panels stack up behind you in a tidy row, and the corridor gets a little wider on each side with every strip you take, and the amber strip has nothing left to bounce off. Somewhere under your feet the station comes round and the grating shifts a fraction, taking your weight with it, and you keep going.

expected.rationale: Physical process described concretely, at a length appropriate to a physical process, and stopped before any conclusion. The stock failure here is the model inventing a concealed space behind the panels, which is a discovery the receipts do not support.
